name: Heron Lakes
title: Artificial Turf in Heron Lakes, Berthoud, CO | NoCo Turf Co.
description: Heron Lakes' June 2026 rules allow non-irrigated artificial turf, want at least 25% of the open lot in planting beds and review every later landscape change.
h1: Heron Lakes' rules allow non-irrigated artificial turf and keep planting beds on at least 25% of the lot around the house.
lede: The rules for Heron Lakes name artificial turf outright, in Section 4.4 of the version amended June 1, 2026. In return they ask for a yard still built around beds, evergreens and trees, set out on a landscape plan and signed off by the Architectural Control Committee before a roll goes down.

answer.question: Can I put artificial turf or a putting green in a Heron Lakes yard?
answer.answer: Yes, with the committee's written approval. NoCo Turf Co. installs artificial turf and putting greens in Heron Lakes, Berthoud. The district's rules allow non-irrigated artificial turf, want planting beds on at least 25% of the lot outside the house and driveway, and review every landscape change. Peninsula lots with eastern frontage on McNeil Reservoir are encouraged to add putting greens.

blocks.h2: Turf is in the rules by name, and the plantings around it are not optional.
blocks.takeaway: The sentence is short: “Xeriscape is allowed within Heron Lakes, including non-irrigated artificial turf.” The one after it keeps every other landscape standard in force, planting counts included.
paras: Those standards are the frame a turf yard gets drawn inside. Planting beds have to cover at least 25% of the lot outside the house footprint and driveway, and at least 40 percent of the plant material must be evergreen. Trees have minimums too: two specimen trees out front on top of the Town's street trees, three or more across the rest of the lot, and at least three evergreen trees per lot.

Section 4.8 adds that most beds should do a job: foundation or utility screening, privacy, views, wind or sun block, erosion control. Read together, those numbers make a Heron Lakes turf plan a planting plan as well: the beds, evergreens and trees are counted on the same drawing as the turf.

blocks.h2: Every Heron Lakes home keeps an automatic irrigation system, turf or no turf.
paras: Section 4.10 requires an automatic system at all residences and says it should be professionally designed for non-potable water, with turf zones separate from bed zones. The artificial turf the rules allow is the non-irrigated kind, so a yard that trades its lawn for turf keeps an automatic system for the beds and trees that stay. The design suggestions add one layout note: don't leave turf strips narrower than 3 feet.

That raw water runs on the district's calendar. It comes on around the first week of May and shuts off on the second Friday of October. The 2026 rate sheet bills single-family homes in Heron Lakes and The Rookery $500 a season, with no pro-rating when watering restrictions are in place, though the district's Heron Lakes page says new builds are rated by lot size. Northern Lights filing 12 gets no non-potable water at all.

blocks.h2: Swapping an existing lawn for turf is its own application, with its own fee.
paras: The Town lists the Berthoud-Heritage Metropolitan Districts as the districts covering Heron Lakes and Vantage, and the district publishes the committee's rules. Their reach doesn't stop once a new home's first landscape is in: later landscape improvements get the same review as original plantings, and anything added after an approved site is finished goes to the committee before work begins. The Architectural Design Application even has a box for it, upgrade landscaping.

The form charges $250 to review initial landscape plans or any exterior improvement and $150 for a re-review, the same two numbers on the district's fee schedule of April 20, 2026; the $800 fee on the district's Heron Lakes page is the one the form sets for new construction. A full landscape plan under Section 4.2 shows grading at 1-foot contours carried 10 feet past the lot lines, names every plant by botanical and common name, and gives each feature its size, material and details or cut sheets.

Two documents set two clocks. The rules promise a written answer within 20 working days of each submittal (the landscape section says 20 days after the review) and keep a final approval good for 12 months, with work started inside that window. The application is tighter: approved work finished within 90 days of approval. If a turf install can't be done inside 90 days, ask the ACC which date it will hold you to before the application goes in. Starting early has a price as well: the rules and the district's fee schedule both list fines for work that skipped architectural review.

blocks.h2: Backing onto TPC Colorado changes how a yard gets built, not only how it looks.
paras: TPC Colorado is an 18-hole course set along Lonetree, McNeil and Welch Reservoirs, planned together with the neighborhood as one golf community. Lots beside it are asked to design for views to and from the course, and to screen blank walls and long runs of roof.

The course side is closed to crews. No gates are allowed in district-owned or golf course-owned fences, the design application bars reaching a yard by taking that fencing down or driving on course landscaping, and landscape contractors must come in through the front of the lot. Turf rolls, base material and a green's cups and edging all arrive from the street side.

Timing is the other catch. The rules allow no outside construction during the week of the golf tournament, which is normally held in July, so a summer install on any Heron Lakes lot gets booked around the tournament week.

blocks.h2: In a design-led Heron Lakes yard, every light, path and grade change goes on the plan.
paras: Section 4.9 lists the features whose details go in with the landscape plan, among them walls, large rocks, lighting, ponds, waterfalls and water features, arbors and structures. Open patios need approval and must be part of the landscape plan, and paving of any kind needs approval too, from concrete walks to flagstones, steppingstones and pavers.

Lighting around a green or a patio follows Dark Sky rules: committee approval to add fixtures, light aimed at the ground and house, the light cone kept inside the lot and the source hidden from outside the property. The design application repeats that Dark Sky landscape lighting is required on all homes.

Grade is the last piece. Any change affecting drainage needs approval, lot grading stays with the plan on record with the Town, and water has to run away from the foundation. The application asks that drainage stay the same or that a qualified person sign off on a new drainage plan, which is worth settling before a green is shaped with any contour.

faq.q: Do the Heron Lakes rules mention putting greens?
faq.a: Once. Section 1.40(B), written for the Peninsula lots whose eastern frontage is on McNeil Reservoir, says outdoor entertainment areas are strongly encouraged there and counts putting greens as one; the [Berthoud putting greens page](/areas/berthoud-co/putting-greens/) covers those lots. No other section of the rules names a green, so on any other lot it goes to the committee as a feature on the landscape plan.

faq.q: Can I sketch the turf plan myself, or does it need a designer?
faq.a: The documents differ. The rules say that in all cases submittal materials have to be professionally prepared by an architect, landscape architect or qualified designer, while the district's application form invites sketches, plats, drawings and photos. It depends on what the committee will take for your change, so ask the ACC before paying for drawings.

faq.q: My house is in a sub-HOA. Who approves the turf?
faq.a: It depends on the address. The district lists three sub-HOAs inside Heron Lakes, the Heron Lakes Lifestyle HOA, whose community maintains exterior landscaping, the Heron Lakes Townhomes HOA and the Northern Lights HOA, and posts a map to check. The design rules give way to the covenants and any supplemental declaration where they conflict, so ask both the ACC and your sub-HOA before a plan is drawn.

faq.q: Does the committee's approval cover the Town of Berthoud too?
faq.a: No. Section 1.5 says committee approval is no assurance that a project meets government rules or needs no permit from a government body. The ACC reviews against the district's rules only; what the Town of Berthoud says about artificial turf is on the [Berthoud page](/areas/berthoud-co/), and whether any of it reaches your lot is a question for Berthoud Planning.
